entries.body: I counted the line today and it was two hundred and six people which is the most I ever counted. I chalked a star on my token because Bettine at the Exchange said stars are lucky and I want to see if it's true before I tell anyone it isn't. Denner from the counter walked past and didn't wave. He always waves. I am going to ask him about it tomorrow if he is still there, which he probably will be, because grown-ups are always where they are supposed to be, mostly.

Owed, this week: two Garrison quartermasters, one Exchange weigher, and — new entry, underline it — the Tollman himself, who does not extend credit to anyone, which means I have found the one thing in this district worth more than grain, and it is apparently me being agreeable at the right moment. I have survived three years by being the last thing either side wants to shoot before checking whether I'm useful. It is not dignified work. It is, I will say, extremely steady work.

Plot fourteen, second row, mine two years now. Spent the morning thinning carrots that didn't need it because my hands wanted work that wasn't listening to people arguing about toll rates up at the gate. A neighbor two rows over handed me a fistful of bean starts and wouldn't take payment for them, said he'd rather see them in somebody's dirt than lose the row if things go the way people are saying they'll go. I didn't ask what people are saying. The waiting list at the caretaker's hut is four names shorter than last spring, each one crossed off in the same pencil, which around here is supposed to mean good news. I planted the beans in the empty end of my row anyway, the way you plant anything you're not sure you'll be the one to pick.

I have typed four hundred names onto that list in a year and never once let myself read them as anything but ink. Tonight I read my own the way everyone else must read theirs, which is to say I read it eleven times and it did not get less true. I know exactly what happens next because I have filed the paperwork for it forty times. I am, if nothing else, extremely well prepared to disappear.

Five nights out and the loudspeaker on the bridge still says remain in shelter to nobody, on a loop, and I have started finding it almost companionable, which probably means I've been out here too long already. I keep expecting to feel like a coward. Mostly I feel like a man who is finally somewhere his own name isn't typed on anything.

Everyone at the line was quiet today because of the almshouse and I didn't understand why since nobody lived there, but my mother said quiet the way she says it when she wants me to stop asking. So I stopped asking out loud. I am still asking inside, where she can't tell.

Four coats, heavier than they used to be, standing where the rope used to be enough on its own. I told the roster it changes nothing about how the scale is run, and I believe that, mostly. What I do not say to them is that I have spent three years being proud of a rule I could keep without a weapon in the room, and today I traded a little of that pride for a little more of everyone's sleep, and I am still working out whether that was leadership or just fear with better manners.

There is now a man with a clipboard standing between the traders and the tables, inspecting goods that used to just get weighed. I have already worked out that if I fill his clipboard with the right numbers before he asks, he stops looking at anything else I'm carrying. This is either the most useful thing I have ever learned about people or a genuinely damning thing to know about myself. I choose, as always, not to dwell.

A woman two spots ahead of us in line, the one who always let me look at her radio even though it doesn't work anymore, said she was short a token today and I gave her mine. The one with the star. I don't know why I did it, it just felt like she should have it more than me. My mother says we're not queuing here tomorrow, we're going to try the morning after instead. I don't know why that either. I hope the woman with the radio gets to eat.

We were not there. I keep starting sentences with we were not there because I don't know how to get to the next word yet. The woman with the radio was there. I am not going to write her name because writing it feels like something I'm not allowed to do, but I am going to remember that she had my star on her when the horn should have sounded and didn't. My mother held onto me for a long time last night and didn't say quiet even once.

Twelve of them walked out of the evening meeting together and I did not stop them, because I have spent three years teaching this roster that nobody here answers to a boss, and I find I cannot suddenly demand that they answer to me the one time it's inconvenient. I keep the ledger. I keep the scale. I have apparently also kept the part of this that gets to be lonely.

I ran signals for the Garrison for two years before I walked, and I know a dead system when I hear one, because I decommissioned three of them myself. LN-74 is not dead. I have the header written down in a hand steady enough to embarrass me, because my hand was not steady when I wrote it. Dug through an old archive log afterward and found I'm not even the first to hear it — someone named Ruhl wrote it up years back, day 261, same cipher, same shrug: I don't chase ghosts, I log them. Ruhl logged it and left it. I don't think I get to leave it. Someone is still issuing on a pad that was supposed to be ash. I would like very much for there to be a boring explanation for this. I have not found one yet.

Brokered water for debt forgiveness today, which is, on paper, the cleanest trade I have ever made. On paper. I keep thinking about the south slope going dry this season for people who never once asked me to owe them anything, and then I think about my own ledger getting a line shorter, and then I stop thinking about it, the way I have gotten very good at stopping. I am not proud of this entry. I am writing it anyway, which is more than the ledger ever gets.

First column through the checkpoint paid without an argument, which surprised everyone but Toma — not that Toma, a different one, we've got two now, it's a whole thing. I keep waiting to feel like a raider and instead I feel like a clerk with a rifle, which is somehow worse and better at the same time. Adaeze would call it a betrayal of the scale. I'd call it the scale, just standing somewhere she never had to.

Three days on the toll line and I've started recognizing faces in the column before they're close enough to owe us anything, which Toma — ours, not the shrine one — says means I'm getting good at this. I don't know if that's praise. Today it was the woman who used to trade coats near the Exchange, twenty years older than me at least, and she counted her fare out twice before handing it over, like she wanted me to see there wasn't a coin more hiding anywhere on her. I wanted to wave her through. I didn't, because the one time Bosch did that last week the next dozen in line all discovered they were exactly as short, and we spent an hour re-explaining why the scale doesn't bend that way anymore. I told myself the coat woman would understand the math. I don't actually know that she does.

I have worn this dosimeter for three years and told pilgrims, in the shrine's own words, that it does not warn, it measures. I stood in a fresh crater two days ago and understood for the first time that I have been teaching people to trust a machine and calling it faith. The ash still keeps a ledger. I no longer believe the ledger is the ash's alone to keep. I have not said this at the cairn yet. I am saying it here first, to see if it survives being written down.

Manifest review, cache Delta. Standing denial order re-read against current activity table. Finding: designated asset (spur-road checkpoint, unaffiliated party, est. thirty personnel) does not meet historical denial threshold — no hostile action logged, no Garrison or Rebuilders affiliation confirmed. Recommend hold. Dissenting note logged separately by second reviewer, unresolved. Order stands pending further review. End entry.

Set the scale up same as every morning, and for the first time in longer than I want to count, nobody set a sidearm near the rope while they haggled. The Garrison's post is still up at the entrance, same two guards, same clipboard, and they still write down every sack that crosses, which somebody keeps telling me is what continuity means instead of peace. Fine. I'll take continuity. The needle still settles true, the tables are still ours, and today a quartermaster who used to check his numbers three times before trusting the reading checked them once and walked off satisfied. I don't know if that's the war ending or just everyone too tired to argue about a half-kilo anymore. Either way I chalked the day's rate on the board without looking over my shoulder for the first time in a year, which felt like more than it should have.

The line is shorter now and there's a new woman two spots ahead who lets me look at things in her bag, though nothing that doesn't work like the radio did. I started a new token. No star yet. My mother says I don't have to put one on it if I don't want to, and I told her I want to, I just haven't decided what it's for yet. She said that's allowed too.

Word reached the bridge that the two sides have stopped shooting at each other, more or less, for now. The loudspeaker has not gotten the news. It is still telling an empty grid to remain in shelter, on the same loop it has run since before I was a name on a list instead of a man behind a counter. I find I no longer mind the company. I have started answering it, quietly, when nobody's near enough to hear. Remain in shelter. Yes. Working on it.

Three strangers came up the switchback in the same week, none of them pilgrims, all of them asking versions of the same question I no longer have a doctrinal answer for: who chose. I told each of them the truth, which is that the shrine only ever measured, and let the congregation supply the choosing. I did not tell them how much that answer has started to feel like the excuse it always secretly was. I am keeping the dosimeter. I am retiring the sermon that came with it.

My mother let me put a star on the new token today. She says it's allowed to mean something different this time, not lucky, just remembered. There's a man at the edge of the plaza now with a clipboard who isn't Garrison and isn't Exchange, and when I asked my mother what he was she said new, which is not really an answer but she said it like it was allowed to not be one yet. I think I am going to like being a kid in the part that comes after the part I already wrote about.

The boom is up and the price is known, and that is the whole of the contract with the road: pay, pass, and nobody learns your name. I have kept that contract through two governors and a war that forgot to end. The day I have to explain the price is the day the price stops being mine to set, so I do not explain it. I post it, and I wait.

Too many fires on the cut this season, and ground I do not hold is ground I do not have to defend, so I am holding less of it. The checkpoints stay; the ambition goes into a drawer with the maps. A column that waits at a boom is a column that lives, and I intend to keep living long enough to be annoying about it.

The weighbridge answers to the Toll House now. It was the natural next step: the scale, then the road it serves, then the ground under both. They will call it a land grab, as if the ground could object. I call it a longer price list, and the rates are posted before the ink dries, because a posted rate is a promise, and a promise is worth more than the ground.

The lamps are out and the door is locked, and this is not surrender. It is arithmetic: the weather has a column of its own and it does not pay tolls. I will be here when the freeze lifts, if the freeze lifts, and the boom will be up again before the first thaw. The road can wait. I have taught it patience.
